source.title: Labeling supervised fine-tuning data with the scaling law

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates downstream task performance across model sizes, using precision and F1 rather than held-out pretraining loss or a compute sweep.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream precision and F1 by model size (Tables 1 and 2), which bear on V6. It does not report a power-law fit to held-out pretraining loss, small-run extrapolation, or a compute-optimal allocation. Table 3 compares fine-tuning methods and hyperparameters at 4B; those optimization comparisons do not test the scaling versions. Figure 3 discusses loss curves for learning-rate settings, not loss scaling with model size, tokens, or compute.
record.test_reason: The paper uses the scaling law as an annotation criterion. Annotators revised prompts and labels until vanilla Qwen precision rose with model size, then cited that trend as proof the annotation is reliable. The precision trend is selected by construction, and the F1 results are the method's own performance on data curated to fit that prior. No result independently tests whether downstream performance scales predictably.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors use the scaling law as the annotation criterion: they re-annotate until vanilla precision rises with size. They then cite that trend, and the post-SFT F1 and precision rising with size (Figure 4), as proof the dataset is reliable. They note the 4B fine-tuning drop is unresolved (lr 2e-5 only reduces it to -3.44) and that LoRA prerequisites need further proof.
record.recipe_differences: Task-specific manual annotation and LoRA fine-tuning evaluated with downstream precision and F1; no held-out pretraining-loss scaling fit, compute sweep, or extrapolation.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that changing the 4B model's learning rate from 2e-4 to 2e-5 mitigated its F1 decline, though the paper does not give a Table 2-style result for that setting.

fits_no_version.finding: On data curated so that vanilla precision rises monotonically with Qwen1.5 size (0.5B-32B), vanilla F1 is non-monotonic: 52.4, 50.0, 62.8, 68.2, 64.6, 60.2. After LoRA SFT, F1 is 60.6, 62.9, 51.3, 69.2, 77.1, 85.6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream metrics on a single small task benchmark need not track model size monotonically, even when one metric is forced to.

record.code_released: The paper says the script and experiments are open-sourced on GitHub, but gives no project URL.
record.problems: Only one downstream task and dataset are evaluated. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The annotation process is iterated until precision increases with model size, which makes that precision trend a selected criterion rather than an independent validation. F1 is non-monotonic, the 4B fine-tuned result drops, and the text gives inconsistent starting F1 values for the MoE result (Table 1: 32.86; abstract: 32.07).
record.rows_left_out: Table 3's comparisons of learning rates, LoRA ranks, and LoRA+ settings for Qwen1.5-4B-Chat are not included: they compare fine-tuning configurations at one model size rather than testing downstream predictability with scale. Figure 3's loss curves are also not included because they compare learning-rate settings, not loss scaling with model size, tokens, or compute.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No shape comparison at fixed size.
No power-law fit for fine-tuning or other regimes.
No independent downstream scaling test: the precision trend is enforced by the annotation loop, and no fit or prediction is made.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests'/T2 and its V6 labels are overturned. The study treats the scaling law as a premise and a filter, not a hypothesis: precision is circular by design, and F1 is the method's own output on a single 2.3k-item task. There are no uncertainty estimates and the MoE starting F1 is inconsistent (32.86 vs 32.07).

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training-regime test of the power-law form.
Tests precision and F1 on one downstream task and dataset; does not test predictability across other tasks or against pretraining loss.
No fitted scaling exponents, compute-optimal split, or comparison of fitting choices and resulting laws.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: F1 scores across vanilla and fine-tuned model sizes, and the differing MoE architecture
reader_labels.reason: F1 is non-monotonic across vanilla sizes and after fine-tuning; the 4B fine-tuned result falls below its vanilla baseline, while MoE is treated by the paper as only a reference. See r2, r4, r6, r8, r10, r12, r14, and r15-r21.
